title: The Three-Day Fever That Was Not
subtitle: The influenza pandemic in camps, cities and colonies, March 1918 – spring 1919
intro: In the autumn of 1918 a disease most doctors had thought of as an unpleasant three-day fever killed, within about twelve weeks, more people than the four years of war then ending. Estimates made long afterwards run from about 17 million to 50 million or more deaths worldwide, with India alone losing somewhere between 12 and 18 million. Unusually, it killed young adults in their twenties and thirties, the age of soldiers, mineworkers and new parents.

Very few of the people in this chapter kept diaries. The honest record of 1918 is mostly letters, official notices, death returns and the reports of inquiries, and the form tags say so. A Kansas doctor's few printed lines, a ward physician's letter from Camp Devens, a painter's note from Vienna and a poet's memoir from the Ganga are set beside city health officers in Philadelphia and Bombay, the US Surgeon General's circular, and the inquiries that New Zealand, South Africa and Britain held when it was over. Several of these voices were first printed long after 1918, and their entries are digests.

The timeline has three waves. A milder one in spring and early summer 1918 was noticed in American army camps, in Spain, whose uncensored press gave the pandemic its misleading name, and in Bombay's docks. The deadly second wave from September to December swept from the camps of Massachusetts and the troopships off Africa to Philadelphia, Kimberley, Bombay, Vienna and, carried by a single steamer, Western Samoa. A third wave in early 1919 killed, among others, Brazil's president-elect Rodrigues Alves, who died in Rio de Janeiro on 16 January 1919 without taking office.

The doctors of 1918 did not know what they were fighting. The leading theory named a bacterium, Pfeiffer's bacillus, found in the throats of many patients; the US Public Health Service taught it, and vaccines were made from it. Experiments on volunteers from a naval detention camp in Boston Harbor failed to transmit the disease at all, and by 1920 the British report called the bacillus unproven and a filter-passing virus possible. Later evidence settled the question: the human influenza virus was isolated in 1933, and the 1918 virus, an H1N1 strain, was sequenced from preserved tissue and reconstructed in 2005. Most deaths, it is now understood, came from bacterial pneumonias following the viral infection, which no medicine of 1918 could cure.

The numbers in these pages were recorded by people who were frightened, exhausted, grieving or defending their decisions. Where a count belongs to a city, an army or an inquiry, the ledger says whose it is. Where the dead were colonised workers in compounds or villagers on a riverbank, the record is thinnest exactly where the losses were greatest.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Many official figures are given by week or by month, and several letters and memoirs are dated only to a month; those entries carry month or range precision. A few city figures were reported by day of publication rather than day of death, so a death count and the day it appears may differ by a day.

eyes.name: Loring Miner
eyes.role: Country physician and county health officer in Haskell County, south-west Kansas, aged about 57
eyes.where: Haskell County, Kansas, on the High Plains
eyes.vantage_label: country doctor who sent the first warning
eyes.authenticity: No diary survives. His warning survives only as a brief item in the US Public Health Service's weekly Public Health Reports of 5 April 1918, a US-government record. The idea that Haskell County was where the pandemic began is a later hypothesis (argued by John M. Barry), not something Miner claimed.
eyes.bio: Miner saw an unusually severe influenza among young, previously healthy patients in the farm county in early 1918 and reported it to the Public Health Service. No investigator was sent. His few lines are the earliest printed American notice of the epidemic, and they show how small the first signal looked.

sources.title: Loring Miner (Wikipedia)
Kansapedia: Flu Pandemic of 1918

eyes.name: US Army Medical Department (camp and Surgeon General's records)
eyes.role: Medical officers of the training camps and the Office of the Surgeon General of the Army
eyes.where: Camp Funston (Fort Riley, Kansas), Camp Devens (Massachusetts) and Washington
eyes.authenticity: Camp sick reports and the Surgeon General's annual reports are US-government records. The day usually given for the first Funston case, 4 March 1918, comes from camp records as summarised by the Army and National Guard; the name of the first patient often printed in popular accounts is not used here because it could not be checked against the record.
eyes.bio: The Army's own figures are the backbone of the American story: a spring outbreak at Camp Funston, then the autumn catastrophe in the eastern camps. Its acting Surgeon General advised against shipping more soldiers while the epidemic raged; President Wilson kept the troopships sailing.

sources.title: National Guard: Flu outbreak killed 45,000 US soldiers during World War I

eyes.name: Roy Grist (signed 'Roy')
eyes.role: US Army physician on Surgical Ward No. 16, base hospital, Camp Devens
eyes.vantage_label: physician on a ward of the dying
eyes.authenticity: A single letter dated 29 September 1918 and signed only 'Roy', to a friend addressed as Burt. It was found decades later and first printed in the British Medical Journal, 22–29 December 1979, under the title 'Camp Devens letter'; the surname Grist comes from that publication. The original is reported to be held in University of Michigan archives. Because it was first published in 1979, entries are digests only.
eyes.bio: Roy wrote at night to a fellow doctor who might soon be posted to Devens, describing what an ordinary-looking flu became within hours. His is the bedside voice of the American camps: overwork, a morgue out of room, and colleagues among the dead.

sources.title: BMJ, 22–29 December 1979: 'Pandemic influenza 1918' (PDF)
Camp Devens Letter (Encyclopedia.com)

eyes.name: Victor Clarence Vaughan
eyes.role: Colonel, US Army Medical Corps, in the Surgeon General's office; dean of the University of Michigan medical school, aged 67
eyes.where: Washington; sent to Camp Devens in late September 1918
eyes.vantage_label: senior investigator sent to the camp
eyes.authenticity: His account of Devens is in his memoir A Doctor's Memories (Indianapolis: Bobbs-Merrill, 1926), written eight years later. English and published before 1929, so a short quotation is allowed, but it is a recollection, not a contemporary record.
eyes.bio: Vaughan was one of the senior physicians the Army sent to Devens when the camp began to fill with dying recruits. He had spent a career on typhoid and sanitation; his memoir is frank that at Devens he did not know what to do.

sources.title: PBS American Experience: Victor Vaughan
Michigan Medicine: 'This infection, like war, kills the young'

eyes.name: Wilmer Krusen
eyes.role: Physician; Director of Public Health and Charities, City of Philadelphia, aged 49
eyes.vantage_label: city health chief who counted the dead
eyes.form: official statements and city returns (as reported in newspapers)
eyes.authenticity: No diary. His decisions and statements survive in city returns and in 1918 Philadelphia newspapers, which are English and pre-1929; only a statement directly quoted in those reports is quoted here.
eyes.bio: Krusen let the Fourth Liberty Loan parade go ahead on 28 September 1918 although the disease was already spreading from the Navy Yard. Within days the city's hospitals were full. His statements track an official trying to reassure a city while the death returns rose.

sources.title: Influenza Encyclopedia (University of Michigan): Philadelphia
Philadelphia Liberty Loans Parade (Wikipedia)

eyes.name: Rupert Lee Blue
eyes.role: Surgeon General of the US Public Health Service, aged 50
eyes.authenticity: His public circular 'Spanish Influenza, Three-Day Fever, The Flu', dated 28 September 1918, is a US-government publication; a copy survives in the Catholic Historical Research Center collections in Philadelphia.
eyes.bio: Blue led the federal health service, which had little money, few staff and no power to close a city. His circular shows the medical consensus of autumn 1918: a named bacillus as the probable cause, rest in bed, and a rhyme about coughs and sneezes.

sources.title: USPHS: Spanish Influenza, Three-Day Fever, The Flu, 28 Sept 1918 (CHRC)
GG Archives transcription of the circular

eyes.name: Milton Joseph Rosenau
eyes.role: Lieutenant-commander, US Navy Medical Corps; Harvard professor of preventive medicine, aged 49
eyes.side: United States Navy and Public Health Service
eyes.where: US quarantine station, Gallops Island, Boston Harbor
eyes.vantage_label: experimenter testing how the disease spread
eyes.authenticity: The experiments were reported in Public Health Reports, vol. 34, no. 2 (10 January 1919), a US-government record, and in Rosenau's article in the Journal of the American Medical Association, vol. 73 (1919). Both are English and pre-1929.
eyes.bio: Rosenau and Public Health Service colleagues tried to give influenza deliberately to volunteers drawn from a naval detention camp in Boston Harbor (men held in naval custody), using bacilli, filtered secretions and the breath of patients. None fell ill. The failure unsettled the Pfeiffer theory without supplying an answer.

sources.title: GG Archives: The Rosenau experiment, 1918–1919
When and Where in Boston: flu tests on Gallops Island

eyes.name: John Andrew Turner
eyes.role: Executive Health Officer of the Municipality of Bombay
eyes.side: British India; Bombay municipal health department
eyes.vantage_label: city health officer of a colonial port
eyes.authenticity: His account survives in his official reports on the Bombay epidemic, quoted by the historian Mridula Ramanna; the figures here are taken from her published study (Scroll.in, 2020, from a chapter in The Spanish Influenza Pandemic of 1918–19: New Perspectives, Routledge, 2003). English and official, pre-1929.
eyes.bio: Turner watched influenza enter Bombay through the docks in the early summer of 1918 and return far worse in the autumn. Bombay counted its dead daily, and his numbers chart the shape of both waves in the city where India's epidemic began.

sources.title: Mridula Ramanna, '1918 Bombay Fever' (Scroll.in, 2020)

eyes.name: Suryakant Tripathi 'Nirala'
eyes.role: Hindi poet, aged about 22, working in Bengal; married to Manohara Devi
eyes.where: Called from Bengal to his in-laws' house at Dalmau on the Ganga, Rae Bareli district
eyes.vantage_label: bereaved husband and son of the family
eyes.authenticity: His account is in the autobiographical book Kulli Bhat (1939), named after a friend he met at Dalmau, written about twenty years after the events; English translation by Satti Khanna as A Life Misspent. Twentieth-century text in translation, so digests only.
eyes.bio: Nirala lost his wife and much of his extended family within weeks in the autumn of 1918. His later account is one of the few literary witnesses to India's pandemic, which killed far more people than anywhere else, mostly in the countryside where few left records.

sources.title: Poems and Chronicles: Nirala and the 1918 influenza (excerpts)
Live History India: Pandemics through the Indian literary lens

eyes.name: Egon Schiele
eyes.role: Painter, aged 28, recently released from army service; married to Edith Schiele (née Harms), who was pregnant
eyes.where: His studio at Wattmanngasse 6, Hietzing, Vienna
eyes.vantage_label: husband at the bedside, then patient
eyes.authenticity: His letter of 27 October 1918 to the painter Broncia Koller-Pinell is in the Leopold Museum, Vienna; his drawings of Edith are dated 27 October 1918. English versions are modern translations, so no quotations.
eyes.bio: Schiele nursed his wife through the last days of her illness, drew her the day before she died, and died himself three days after her. His few lines to friends are among the clearest private records of the second wave in Vienna, in the last week of the Habsburg empire.

sources.title: Leopold Museum: letter from Egon Schiele to Broncia Koller-Pinell, 27 Oct 1918
Wellcome Collection: art of the 1918 flu

eyes.name: Samoan Epidemic Commission (New Zealand), 1919
eyes.role: Commission of inquiry appointed by the New Zealand government into the epidemic in the occupied territory of Western Samoa
eyes.side: New Zealand administration of Western Samoa; Samoan witnesses
eyes.authenticity: The commission's report was presented to the New Zealand Parliament in 1919 and summarised in New Zealand newspapers in August 1919 (Papers Past). Official English text, pre-1929. Samoan survivors' own accounts were mostly recorded much later and are not used here.
eyes.bio: The commission reconstructed how the steamer Talune brought the disease to Apia on 7 November 1918 and how about a fifth of the people of Western Samoa died within weeks. Its report assigned fault to officials in Auckland and Apia and to the ship's master, and records the contrast with American Samoa, which had closed its ports.

sources.title: DigitalNZ: The 1918 influenza pandemic in Samoa and the wider Pacific
SS Talune (Wikipedia)
Influenza 1918: the Samoan experience

eyes.name: Influenza Epidemic Commission, Union of South Africa
eyes.role: Government commission of inquiry into the epidemic, reporting in Cape Town in 1919
eyes.where: Cape Town and the mining towns, especially Kimberley
eyes.vantage_label: official inquiry counting the dead by place and race
eyes.authenticity: Report of the Influenza Epidemic Commission (Cape Town, 1919), an official English publication, pre-1929. The Kimberley mortality figures here are as cited from it and from mining records by later studies (PMC 7314043; Howard Phillips, Black October, 1990).
eyes.bio: South Africa suffered one of the worst death rates outside the Pacific, and the inquiry recorded it unevenly: the diamond-mine compounds of Kimberley lost far more than the gold mines of the Rand. It is the official eye on what South Africans came to call Black October.

sources.title: Shanks et al., mortality in South African mining populations (PMC)
Howard Phillips, Black October (UCT thesis)

eyes.name: British Ministry of Health (Report on the Pandemic of Influenza, 1918–19)
eyes.role: Ministry of Health, London; introduction by George Newman, Chief Medical Officer, addressed to the Minister, Christopher Addison
eyes.authenticity: Reports on Public Health and Medical Subjects No. 4 (London: HMSO, 1920); the introduction is dated October 1920. English and pre-1929, so short quotation is allowed. A digitised copy is held by the Wellcome Collection.
eyes.bio: The British report pulled together death returns, laboratory work and evidence from the empire and allies. It is the most careful official account of what the doctors of 1918 believed and doubted about the cause.

sources.title: Wellcome Collection: Report on the pandemic of influenza, 1918–19
GG Archives: summary of the 1920 report

eyes.name: The press in Madrid (Spanish dailies and foreign correspondents)
eyes.role: Newspapers of a neutral country without wartime censorship of epidemic news
eyes.side: Spain (neutral in the First World War)
eyes.authenticity: Spanish dailies of May–June 1918 and the report of The Times correspondent in Madrid (3 June 1918). Spanish texts appear here only as digests; the press nicknames are given as short phrases.
eyes.bio: Because Spain was neutral, its papers printed the epidemic openly in May 1918, while the belligerents kept their own outbreaks quiet. The result was the name 'Spanish' influenza, which stuck although the disease had not started there.

sources.title: Ayuntamiento de Madrid: La gripe española, un siglo después
El Español: Alfonso XIII and the flu

entries.headline: A country doctor sees a fierce new influenza
entries.digest: Miner's practice in the thinly settled county filled with patients struck down by a violent influenza, many of them young and healthy adults rather than the old. Some developed pneumonia and died. He alerted the US Public Health Service; nobody came to investigate.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia 'Loring Miner'; Kansapedia notes a local doctor's report and no investigation. Month approximate: the outbreak is placed in late winter 1918 in secondary accounts.

entries.headline: First influenza cases reported at Camp Funston
entries.digest: Medical officers at Camp Funston, a vast training camp of about 56,000 men on the Fort Riley reservation, identified the first cases of an influenza outbreak. Recruits slept crowded in barracks and tents through a cold Kansas spring, and men moved constantly between camp, other bases and the ports for France.
entries.source_note: National Guard article (2018), citing Army records: first cases identified 4 March 1918.

entries.headline: 1,100 soldiers sick in three weeks
entries.digest: Within about three weeks of the first cases, some 1,100 of the camp's 56,222 troops had been admitted sick. The outbreak was severe enough to be noted but was not treated as exceptional; soldiers kept moving east and overseas.
entries.source_note: National Guard article: 1,100 of 56,222 sick within three weeks. End date of the three weeks approximate.

entries.headline: A few printed lines from Kansas
entries.digest: The weekly Public Health Reports printed a short notice from Haskell, Kansas: eighteen cases of influenza of a severe type, three of them fatal. It is the earliest mention of the epidemic in the federal health service's journal, a few lines among routine notices.
entries.source_note: Public Health Reports, 5 April 1918, as summarised by Historydraft ('18 severe cases and death tally of three in Haskell, Kansas'). Exact wording not checked against the issue.

entries.headline: Madrid's papers report an epidemic openly
entries.digest: Madrid newspapers reported a fast-spreading illness in the capital in May 1918 and gave it nicknames: 'the soldier of Naples', after a catchy song in a popular zarzuela, and 'the illness of the day'. At one point a large share of Madrid's people were said to be ill. Unlike the warring countries, Spain had no military censorship suppressing the news.
entries.source_note: Ayuntamiento de Madrid blog (2020) on press nicknames; El Español (2020) on May 1918 as the first officially documented case in Madrid.

entries.headline: The king himself falls ill
entries.digest: King Alfonso XIII, aged 32, fell seriously ill with the epidemic, as did members of the government. The king's illness was reported in the press, which made the outbreak international news and helped fix the idea that Spain was its source.
entries.source_note: El Español (2020) places the illness within March–July 1918; late May–June is the period most accounts give. Exact days not verified.

entries.headline: A ship's crew brings the fever ashore
entries.digest: Turner later traced Bombay's outbreak to the crew of a ship that docked at the end of May. He described how suddenly the disease appeared in a city that had no warning of it.
entries.quote: came like a thief at night
entries.source_note: Turner as quoted by Ramanna (Scroll.in, 2020); the quotation is from his official report (English, pre-1929). Ship's arrival date given only as end of May.

entries.headline: Seven police sepoys, then the mills
entries.digest: The first recognised cases were seven police sepoys admitted to hospital with a fever that was not malaria. Between 15 and 20 June workers fell sick at the Port Trust, the Dockyard, the Telegraph office, the Mint and the Rachel Sassoon Mills. The first wave lasted about four weeks and killed around 1,600 people.
entries.source_note: Ramanna (Scroll.in, 2020), from municipal health reports.

entries.headline: London hears of a 'Spanish' epidemic
entries.digest: The Times of London carried a report from its Madrid correspondent on the epidemic sweeping Spain. Madrid's own historians credit this report with spreading the label 'Spanish influenza' abroad, although the same illness was already moving through the armies in France.
entries.source_note: Ayuntamiento de Madrid blog (2020) dates The Times correspondent's report to 3 June 1918; the Times text was not consulted.

entries.headline: First wave peaks at 230 deaths a day
entries.digest: Daily deaths in Bombay rose from 92 on 21 June to 230 on 3 July, then fell away. The city's health service and private relief groups had little to offer beyond hospital beds and food; Turner's figures recorded the curve as it rose and broke.
entries.source_note: Ramanna (Scroll.in, 2020).

entries.headline: A mild summer wave
entries.digest: The 1920 report later dated the first English wave to the end of June 1918, peaking in the first half of July and fading by the end of the month. It was widely regarded at the time as a short, unpleasant 'three-day fever', with few deaths.
entries.source_note: Ministry of Health, Report on the Pandemic of Influenza (1920), as summarised by GG Archives.

entries.headline: The Salamis reaches Durban
entries.digest: The troopship Salamis arrived at Durban from Somalia, and several hundred harbour workers fell ill with what was diagnosed as simple influenza. Ships with similar mild illness had been arriving in Durban and Cape Town since July; the much deadlier wave reached Cape Town on troopships later in September.
entries.source_note: PMC 7314043, citing the Influenza Epidemic Commission report (1919).

entries.headline: Beds for the Navy, and reassurance
entries.digest: With sailors from the Navy Yard falling ill, Krusen reserved 150 beds at the Municipal Hospital for Contagious Diseases for the Navy. He told Philadelphians there was nothing to fear if cases were strictly isolated. The next day reports said the Naval Hospital had taken 400 new cases in three days, and he still predicted few deaths.
entries.source_note: Influenza Encyclopedia (University of Michigan), Philadelphia essay.

entries.headline: Orders to Devens: the wards overflow
entries.digest: Vaughan arrived at Camp Devens under urgent orders with other senior Army physicians on a cold, drizzly morning. He saw strong young recruits streaming into wards already full, men with a bluish cast to their faces coughing blood-stained sputum. That day 63 men died of influenza in the camp.
entries.quote: hundreds of young stalwart men in uniform coming into the wards
entries.source_note: Vaughan, A Doctor's Memories (1926), as quoted by PBS American Experience and Michigan Medicine. The day is the one usually given for the visit; the sources consulted say only 'September 1918'.

entries.headline: The Liberty Loan parade goes ahead
entries.digest: Krusen allowed the Fourth Liberty Loan parade to march down Broad Street, despite the doubts of many local physicians. More than 200,000 people crowded the route to watch bands, troops and floats. The parade was a patriotic bond drive; cancelling it would have meant admitting a crisis the city had not yet declared.
entries.source_note: Influenza Encyclopedia, Philadelphia; Wikipedia 'Philadelphia Liberty Loans Parade' (attendance over 200,000).

entries.headline: Federal advice: bed, isolation, and a rhyme
entries.digest: Blue's circular explained that a small rod-shaped germ, Pfeiffer's bacillus, had been found in many cases, along with pneumonia germs, and that the disease was believed to spread from person to person through droplets from coughing, sneezing and talking. It advised the sick to go to bed, to keep others out of the room, to burn discharges, and for nurses to wear gowns and masks.
entries.quote: Cover up each cough and sneeze
entries.source_note: USPHS circular dated 28 September 1918 (CHRC item 8215); text via GG Archives transcription. US-government record.

entries.headline: 'About 100 deaths per day'
entries.digest: Roy wrote to his friend Burt that the camp was averaging about a hundred deaths a day. Men came in with what looked like ordinary grippe and within hours had a severe pneumonia; dark spots appeared on the cheeks and a blue colour spread across the face before death. His ward had 168 beds; the number of doctors in the camp had gone from about 25 to over 250, and some of them, and nurses, had died. Bodies filled the morgue faster than they could be sent away.
entries.source_note: Letter dated 29 September 1918, printed in BMJ 22–29 December 1979 (digest only); PBS and Encyclopedia.com summaries.

entries.headline: A quarter of Camp Devens sick
entries.digest: By the end of September about 14,000 soldiers at Camp Devens had fallen ill, roughly a quarter of the camp, and 757 had died. The acting Surgeon General recommended halting troop shipments to France until the epidemic passed; President Wilson decided to keep them going.
entries.source_note: National Guard article (2018), citing Army figures.

entries.headline: Theatres, saloons, schools and churches close
entries.digest: Five days after the parade, the state health commissioner, Franklin Royer, ordered places of public amusement closed from midnight, and the Philadelphia Board of Health closed schools and churches, with 4,000 pupils reported sick. Two days earlier the mayor had placed a $100,000 emergency fund at Krusen's disposal. All the city's hospital beds were already full.
entries.source_note: Influenza Encyclopedia, Philadelphia.

entries.headline: 768 deaths in a single day
entries.digest: The second wave in Bombay rose from 219 deaths on 16 September to 768 on 6 October. It struck hardest among the poor in crowded tenements. Private relief committees, volunteers and caste and community organisations ran dispensaries and distributed food, while critics accused the colonial government of neglect.
entries.source_note: Ramanna (Scroll.in, 2020).

entries.headline: 'Reached its crest' – too soon
entries.digest: After more than 5,500 new cases were reported in a single day, Krusen announced that the epidemic had peaked. It had not: deaths kept rising for nearly two weeks, and trucks were soon carrying bodies from the city morgue to a potter's field.
entries.quote: Epidemic influenza in Philadelphia has reached its crest
entries.source_note: Statement quoted in the Influenza Encyclopedia essay (from 1918 Philadelphia newspapers). Date as given there; not re-checked against the newspaper.

entries.headline: Black October in the diamond town
entries.digest: In October the epidemic swept Kimberley. Among De Beers diamond miners, mostly black migrant workers housed in closed compounds, the death rate exceeded 22 per cent that month, against about 0.6 per cent among Witwatersrand gold miners; in the Kimberley gaol 15.5 per cent of prisoners died. Mortality in the Cape Province overall was about three times that in Natal.
entries.source_note: PMC 7314043, from mining and commission records.

entries.place: Bengal, then Dalmau on the Ganga
entries.headline: A telegram: his wife is gravely ill
entries.digest: Nirala received a telegram saying his young wife, Manohara Devi, was gravely ill at her parents' house in Dalmau. By the time he arrived she had died. In the following days the epidemic went through his family: his cousin, his uncle (the head of the household), his sister-in-law and a nursing child died, along with labourers who worked the family's land.
entries.source_note: Kulli Bhat (1939), as excerpted in Satti Khanna's translation (Poems and Chronicles, 2020). Month approximate; the account gives no exact dates.

entries.headline: The river full of the dead
entries.digest: He remembered sitting on a mound above the Ganga at Dalmau, watching corpses being brought down to the river one after another. India's dead were counted afterwards in millions, but most left no record of their own.
entries.source_note: Kulli Bhat (1939) excerpts via Poems and Chronicles; Live History India. Written about twenty years later.

entries.headline: 606 deaths and 1,300 new cases
entries.digest: The city reported more than 1,300 new cases and 606 deaths in a day. Coffins ran short, and families waited days to bury their dead. Ten days later the daily count had fallen to 125 new cases and 317 deaths.
entries.source_note: Influenza Encyclopedia, Philadelphia.

entries.headline: 'Prepared for the worst'
entries.digest: Schiele wrote to the painter Broncia Koller-Pinell that Edith had grown worse: constant nausea, great difficulty breathing, and injections on the two previous days. He wrote that her fate would be decided within a day and that he was ready for the worst. The same day he made his last drawings of her face.
entries.source_note: Leopold Museum, object 35114 (letter dated 27 October 1918); Wellcome Collection article on the drawing dated 27 October 1918.

entries.headline: Edith Schiele dies, six months pregnant
entries.digest: Edith died the morning after the drawings, carrying their first child. Schiele sent his sister Gerti a short, flat note announcing her death. He was already ill himself. That day Czechoslovakia declared independence in Prague; the empire around Vienna was breaking apart.
entries.source_note: Wellcome Collection; R. H. Carpenter's account of the note to Gerti. Pregnancy as reported in standard biographies.

entries.headline: Schiele dies three days after Edith
entries.digest: Schiele died of the same illness, aged 28, three days after his wife. His mother and his sister Melanie visited him at the end. He left no further writing; the record of his last days is his family's.
entries.source_note: Wellcome Collection (death 31 October 1918); Carpenter (family visit).

entries.headline: The Talune sails for the islands
entries.digest: The Union Steam Ship Company's Talune left Auckland, where the epidemic was spreading, with several crew members already ill. No wireless warning reached Apia, and her bill of health did not record that influenza was rife in Auckland, both points the commission later laid at New Zealand's door.
entries.source_note: Corpus.nz, 'Influenza 1918: the Samoan experience'; DigitalNZ; Talune departure date from corpus.nz.

entries.headline: The autumn wave peaks
entries.digest: The 1920 report dated the second English wave from October, with deaths peaking in the first week of November and falling slowly through December. It was by far the deadliest of the three, accounting for about three-quarters of the influenza deaths counted in the 46 weeks from late June 1918. The peak fell in the week of the Armistice.
entries.source_note: Ministry of Health report (1920), via GG Archives.

entries.headline: Pratique granted: passengers walk ashore
entries.digest: The Talune reached Apia from Fiji, where she had been held in quarantine alongside the wharf and had taken on about 90 Fijian labourers, most of whom were sick by arrival. The acting port health officer, unaware of the Auckland epidemic, granted pratique after a cursory check, and passengers disembarked. Within days the disease spread through the islands.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia 'SS Talune'; DigitalNZ; NZ commission findings as summarised there.

entries.headline: Volunteers exposed to the disease
entries.digest: Rosenau's team began trying to infect volunteers from a US naval detention training camp in Boston Harbor. The men, held in naval custody, were sprayed and swabbed with cultures of Pfeiffer's bacillus and with filtered and unfiltered secretions from patients, injected with patients' blood, and made to sit beside and breathe with men sick in the Chelsea Naval Hospital. Similar work was done at Angel Island, San Francisco.
entries.source_note: GG Archives, 'The Rosenau Experiment', from Public Health Reports 34:2 (1919). Promises of pardons to the volunteers, often repeated, are not supported by this source.

entries.headline: At least 7,542 dead by the year's end
entries.digest: By the end of December at least 7,542 people had died in Western Samoa, and the commission later estimated about 8,500, around 22 per cent of the population; the deaths fell heavily on adults aged 18 to 50 and on chiefs and pastors. Administrator Robert Logan had declined an offer of medical help from American Samoa, under 50 km away. There, Governor John Poyer had imposed a strict quarantine without orders from Washington, and no one died of influenza.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia 'SS Talune' (7,542 by 31 Dec; ~8,500 estimate; Poyer); DigitalNZ (Logan's refusal of help); corpus.nz (age groups).

entries.headline: 45,000 soldiers dead of influenza and pneumonia
entries.digest: Army figures counted about 45,000 American soldiers dead of influenza and its pneumonias by the end of 1918, close to the number killed in combat. Most died in camps in the United States, not in France.
entries.source_note: National Guard article (2018). The comparison with combat deaths depends on which totals are used.

entries.headline: No volunteer caught the disease
entries.digest: Public Health Reports published the results under a frank title: some interesting though unsuccessful attempts to transmit influenza experimentally. Not one volunteer in the Boston trials developed influenza, whatever was done to them. The authors drew no conclusion about the cause.
entries.source_note: Public Health Reports 34:2 (10 January 1919), pp. 33–36, per GG Archives.

entries.headline: Brazil's president-elect dies of the epidemic
entries.digest: Francisco de Paula Rodrigues Alves, elected president of Brazil on 1 March 1918, had been too ill to take office on 15 November and died of influenza in Rio de Janeiro on 16 January 1919. His vice-president, Delfim Moreira, governed in his place. The news ran in papers across the Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking world.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia 'Rodrigues Alves' for dates. Assignment to this press eye is an editorial grouping; Madrid coverage of the death was not checked.

entries.headline: A third wave
entries.digest: A third wave began in early February 1919, peaked in the third week of the month and declined slowly through March. The count ended on 10 May 1919.
entries.source_note: Ministry of Health report (1920), via GG Archives.

entries.headline: The inquiry: 'a blunder which amounts to a crime'
entries.digest: The commission's findings, reported in New Zealand papers in August 1919, faulted the New Zealand authorities for failing to warn Apia, the port health officer for granting pratique, the Talune's master for not declaring illness on board, and Administrator Logan for a range of failures. A senior missionary told the commission the response had been worse than a mistake.
entries.quote: a blunder which amounts to a crime
entries.source_note: Corpus.nz and DigitalNZ summaries of the commission; Papers Past newspaper reports of 18–19 August 1919. Missionary's words as quoted in corpus.nz; month of publication from newspaper dates.

entries.headline: 'Not quite sure what we know'
entries.digest: Writing up the experiments for American physicians, Rosenau admitted that months of careful work had produced only negative results. The confident textbook picture of a known germ had not survived the test, and he said so plainly.
entries.quote: we are not quite sure what we know about the disease
entries.source_note: Rosenau, JAMA 73 (1919), p. 311, quoted by GG Archives. Issue date not verified; year only.

entries.headline: The Union's report is published
entries.digest: The Influenza Epidemic Commission published its report in Cape Town in 1919. It compared mortality region by region, recording among other things that the Cape Province suffered about three times the death rate of Natal.
entries.source_note: PMC 7314043 cites the report (Cape Town, 1919) and its Natal–Cape comparison.

entries.headline: 151,446 dead, and the cause still unproven
entries.digest: Newman's introduction, dated October 1920, set out the toll: the Registrar-General attributed 151,446 deaths in England and Wales to influenza in the 46 weeks from 23 June 1918 to 10 May 1919. The report said Pfeiffer's bacillus was associated with the disease but its role as cause remained unproven; Sir Frederick Andrewes called it a major secondary invader, and evidence for a filter-passing virus was suggestive but not conclusive.
entries.source_note: Ministry of Health, Report on the Pandemic of Influenza 1918–19 (HMSO, 1920), via GG Archives; Wellcome Collection copy.

claims.claim: First influenza cases identified at Camp Funston, Kansas; about 1,100 of 56,222 troops sick within three weeks
claims.evidence: Army records as summarised by the National Guard (2018)

claims.claim: Eighteen cases of severe influenza, three fatal, reported from Haskell, Kansas
claims.evidence: Public Health Reports, 5 April 1918 (summary via Historydraft)

claims.claim: Bombay's first recognised cases: seven police sepoys; first wave about 1,600 deaths in four weeks
claims.evidence: Bombay municipal health reports, via Ramanna (2020)

claims.claim: Start of the 46-week count that later totalled 151,446 influenza deaths in England and Wales
claims.evidence: Registrar-General's returns in the 1920 Ministry of Health report

claims.claim: Troopship Salamis at Durban; several hundred harbour workers ill with what was called simple influenza
claims.evidence: Influenza Epidemic Commission report (1919), cited in PMC 7314043

claims.claim: Pfeiffer's bacillus found in many cases and treated as the probable cause; disease spread person to person by droplets (the view of the time; the virus was first isolated in 1933)
claims.evidence: USPHS circular 'Spanish Influenza, Three-Day Fever, The Flu'

claims.claim: Liberty Loan parade allowed; more than 200,000 spectators on Broad Street
Camp Devens averaging about 100 deaths a day; doctors increased from about 25 to over 250
About 14,000 sick (a quarter of the camp) and 757 dead at Camp Devens
Death rate above 22% among De Beers miners at Kimberley in one month, against about 0.6% on the Witwatersrand gold mines; 15.5% in Kimberley gaol
768 deaths in Bombay in one day, up from 219 on 16 September
606 deaths and over 1,300 new cases in Philadelphia in one day; excess death rate for the epidemic 748 per 100,000
Talune granted pratique at Apia; about 8,500 deaths (about 22% of Western Samoa) followed, against none in quarantined American Samoa
claims.evidence: Samoan Epidemic Commission findings; Wikipedia 'SS Talune'; DigitalNZ

claims.claim: No volunteer infected in the Boston transmission experiments using Pfeiffer's bacillus, filtered secretions and patient contact (later evidence: influenza is a virus spread by respiratory droplets and aerosols; the negative result remains unexplained in detail)
Pfeiffer's bacillus as cause 'remains unproven'; filter-passing virus suggestive but not conclusive (later evidence: human influenza virus isolated 1933; the 1918 H1N1 virus reconstructed in 2005)
claims.evidence: Ministry of Health, Report on the Pandemic of Influenza 1918–19 (1920)

convergences.label: Spring 1918: the first American signals
convergences.note: A Kansas army camp and a Kansas country doctor recorded severe influenza within weeks of each other, and both reports went to Washington without alarm. Whether the two outbreaks were connected, as some historians argue, is a later hypothesis, not something either recorded.

convergences.label: Late May – June 1918: the disease gets its name
convergences.note: Madrid's uncensored papers made the epidemic visible just as Bombay's docks and England's towns met the same mild first wave. The name 'Spanish' came from openness, not origin.

convergences.label: Week of 23–29 September 1918: the autumn wave breaks over America
convergences.note: In one week a senior Army investigator walked the Devens wards, a ward doctor wrote of a hundred deaths a day, Philadelphia's health chief let 200,000 people gather for a parade, and the Surgeon General issued advice built on a germ that was not the cause. The same facts were known at Devens and not acted on in Philadelphia.

convergences.label: October 1918: 'Black October' on three continents
convergences.note: Bombay's 768 deaths in a day, Kimberley's compounds, Philadelphia's full morgues and Nirala's family at Dalmau belong to the same few weeks. The official counts measured the cities; Nirala's memory is the countryside that the counts barely reached.

convergences.label: End of October 1918: Vienna, Philadelphia, Auckland
convergences.note: As Schiele died in Vienna and Philadelphia reopened its theatres on 30 October, the Talune sailed from Auckland for Fiji and Samoa, carrying the wave toward people who had not yet met it.

convergences.label: Armistice week: the peak in England, the arrival in Samoa
convergences.note: England's deaths peaked in the first week of November; on 7 November the Talune landed passengers at Apia; on 13 November Rosenau began trying to infect volunteers in Boston Harbor. Peace in Europe coincided with the pandemic's spread to the Pacific.

convergences.label: The cause in question: bacillus or something smaller
convergences.note: Blue's circular named Pfeiffer's bacillus; Rosenau's failed experiments undermined it; the British report of 1920 called it unproven and a filterable virus suggestive. Each reported what it could test; the virus was isolated only in 1933.

ties.note: Both were at Camp Devens in the last days of September 1918: Vaughan inspecting the hospital, Roy working one of its wards.
Vaughan served as a colonel in the Surgeon General's office, and his reports from the camps fed the Army's own record of the epidemic.
Roy's hundred-a-day figure is a ward doctor's version of the Devens deaths the Army counted officially (757 by the end of September).
Haskell County and Camp Funston are both in Kansas, about 300 miles apart; some historians argue that draftees from the county carried the disease to the camp, a position, not a proven route.
Blue's federal circular, dated the day of the Liberty Loan parade, was distributed in Philadelphia; a copy survives in a Philadelphia collection.
Rosenau's team included Public Health Service officers, and Blue's service published the negative results in its own journal in January 1919.
Blue's 1918 circular treated Pfeiffer's bacillus as the likely cause; the 1920 British report concluded its role was unproven. Two positions held two years apart, on the same evidence base.
Both describe India's epidemic, Turner in a port city's daily returns, Nirala in a village where no one was counting; the national toll ran to many millions.
Two dominion inquiries of 1919 that recorded the highest death rates among colonised peoples: Samoans in Western Samoa, black mineworkers in Kimberley.
Two city health officers in port cities counting daily deaths in the same October, one in an American city with its own powers, the other in a colonial municipality under criticism for neglect.

threads_out.note: Philadelphia met its two worst epidemics 125 years apart, yellow fever in 1793 and influenza in 1918; in both, city officials, physicians and citizens' committees argued over gatherings, burials and how much to tell the public.

Bombay's municipal health department, created and strengthened during the plague years from 1896, was the office that counted the city's influenza dead in 1918, in the same crowded tenements and docks.
Thomas Francis Jr., who developed early influenza vaccines with Jonas Salk in the Army-funded work that followed 1918, went on to direct the 1954 field trial of Salk's polio vaccine.

The autumn wave travelled with armies: training camps such as Devens and Funston, troopships to France and South Africa, and the last offensives of 1918; about as many American soldiers died of influenza and pneumonia as in battle.
The pandemic's third wave reached the Paris Peace Conference; President Wilson fell seriously ill in early April 1919 in the middle of the negotiations.
